raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|turn|6538|turn}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|This house is ''turned'' upside down since Robin Ostler died.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 1. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I talke and prate, and lay ’t not on their jackes,
And the proud Jacks care not a fig for me;
But bones a me, Ile ''turne'' another leafe.</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', If you Know not me (Works, ed. 1874, I. 257).}}}}
{{smaller block|When she [the hen] has laid her eggs in such a manner that she can cover them, what care does she take in ''turning'' them frequently, that all parts may partake of the vital warmth.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 120.}}}}
'''10.''' To throw; overthrow; overturn.
{{smaller block|All Troy for to take and ''tirne'' at hor wille.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4508.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Troiens with tene thai ''tirnyt'' to ground,
Kyld of hor knightes & comyns full mony.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 10282.}}}}
'''11†.''' To set.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Troiens thaire tore shippis hade ''turnyt'' on ffyre,
Wold haue brent hom barly, botis & other.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7112.}}}}
'''12†.''' To return; send back.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tell her I sent it to make merry with,
She’ll ''turn'' us thanks at least!</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, i. 2.}}}}
'''13.''' To transfer; put into other hands; turn over.
{{smaller block|Our inheritance is ''turned'' to strangers, our houses to aliens.
{{right|Lam. v. 2.}}}}
'''14.''' To fold so that the other side may appear: as, to ''turn'' down one’s collar.—'''15.''' To remake with the inside turned out; make over again by reversing the material: as, to ''turn'' a garment.
{{smaller block|A pair of old breeches thrice ''turned''.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 2. 44.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mrs. Cratchit, . . . dressed out but poorly in a twice-''turned'' gown.
{{right|''Dickens'', Christmas Carol, iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Her satin gown had been ''turned'' and made over till every possible capability of it was exhausted.
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 51.}}}}

'''16.''' To change to another opinion or party; change with respect to convictions, sentiments, feelings, or conduct; convert or pervert.

{{smaller block|One suffering for the truth ''turneth'' more than a thousand sermons.
{{right|''Latimer'', Misc. Sel.}}}}

<poem>Will nothing ''turn'' your unrelenting hearts?</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 4. 59.}}}}

<poem>So, ''turn'', good Lord, O ''turn'' the hearts of Princes,
Whose Rage their realms with Saints deer bloud berinses.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Bethulians Rescue, vi.}}}}

<poem>Wisest woman
That ever tipped her tongue with point of reasons,
To ''turn'' her hearers!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Magnetick Lady, iv. 2.}}}}

'''17.''' To change or alter the nature, character, or appearance of in any way; change into something else; transform; transmute; metamorphose.

<poem>Watir to wyne he ''turned'' ryue,
He garte corne growe with-outen plogh,
Wher are was none.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''York Plays'', p. 205.}}}}

{{smaller block|There an Aungel helde Jacob stille, and ''turned'' his Name, and cleped him Israel.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 86.}}}}

{{smaller block|There was sometime in Œæa a woman called Circe, which by enchantment . . . used with a drink to ''turn'' as many men as received it into divers likeness and figures of sundry beasts.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Life of Picus (Utopia, Int., p. lxxxi.).}}}}

{{smaller block|You may as well go about to ''turn'' the sun to ice with fanning in his face with a peacock’s feather.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 1. 212.}}}}

<poem>They ’ll ''turn'' me in your arms, Janet,
An adder and an ask.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''The Young Tamlane'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 122).}} Nay, must my mirth be so suddenly ''turned'' into bitter howlings, and my ease into a bed of flames?
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. xi.}}}}

'''18.''' To change from one language or form of expression to another; paraphrase; translate; construe.
{{smaller block|Most of these things we had from his own mouth, and heard him ''turn'' the oriental languages into Latin very readily. ''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 233.

At the age of eleven [Emerson] was ''turning'' Virgil into very readable English heroics. ''O. W. Holmes'', Emerson, i.}}

'''19.''' To change from a fresh, sweet, or otherwise natural condition; cause to ferment, become sour, or the like: as, warm weather ''turns'' milk.
{{smaller block|<poem>You’ve almost ''turned'' my good affection to you;
Soured my sweet thoughts, all my pure purposes.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Devil is an Ass, ii. 3.}}}}

'''20.''' To put or bring into a certain state or condition: as, the wine has ''turned'' him sick.
{{smaller block|A slave that still . . . ''turns'' me to shame.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 4. 67.}}

Should I tell you gravely that without the help of coins we should never have known which was the first of the emperors that wore a beard, or rode in stirrups, I might ''turn'' my science into ridicule.
{{right|''Addison'', Dialogues on Medals, i.}}}}

'''21†.''' To get around; trick; beguile; cheat.
{{smaller block|Til he had ''torned'' him he coude not blinne.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 160.}}}}

'''22.''' To render unbalanced or unsound; distract: as, to ''turn'' one’s head. See the phrase below.—'''Not to turn a hair.''' {{smaller|See ''hair''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''To be turned,''' or {{smaller|'''to be turned of''', to be or to have advanced beyond: said with regard to age.}}
{{smaller block|Irus, though he ''is'' now ''turned of'' fifty, has not appeared in the world in his real character since five-and-twenty.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 264.}}}}
{{smaller block|When they [miners] ''are turned of'' thirty they begin to look thin, and are much subject to plurisies and palsies.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 227.}}}}
{{smaller block|Of late, trouble of another kind has been added. Tina ''is'' a little ''turned of'' fifteen; she is going to be very beautiful.
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 406.}}}}

'''To turn a cat-in-pan.''' {{smaller|See ''cat''<sup>1</sup>.}}—'''To turn adrift.''' {{smaller|See ''adrift''.}}—'''To turn against.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To use to the disadvantage or injury of: as, his argument was ''turned against'' himself; they ''turned'' their arms ''against'' their friends. (''b'') To render unfriendly or opposed to: as, his old comrade was ''turned against'' him by false reports.}}—'''To turn an enemy’s flank line,''' or '''position,''' {{smaller|to manœuver so as to pass round his forces and attack him from the rear or on the flank; hence,}} '''to turn one’s flank,''' {{smaller|in a figurative sense, to circumvent or outwit one.}}
{{smaller block|Tom felt at once that his ''flank'' was ''turned''.
{{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|A number of attempts were made by the enemy to ''turn'' our right ''flank'', where Sherman was posted, but every effort was repulsed with heavy loss.
{{right|''U. S. Grant'', Personal Memoirs, I. 339.}}}}

'''To turn a penny.''' {{smaller|See ''penny''.}}—'''To turn aside,''' {{smaller|to turn to one side; ward off; avert: as, to ''turn aside'' a blow or a thrust.}}—'''To turn away.''' {{smaller|(''a'') To turn in an opposite or different direction; avert.}}
{{smaller block|She ''turns away'' the face.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1711.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') To turn aside; avert.}}
{{smaller block|We pray to God to ''turn away'' some evil from us.
{{right|''Whole Duty of Man.''}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') To dismiss from service; discharge; discard.}}
{{smaller block|I must ''turn away'' some of my followers.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 3. 4.}} The Master of the House may ''turn away'' all his Servants, and take whom he please. {{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 63.}}}}
'''To turn back.''' (''a'') To cause to return or retrace one’s footsteps: as, I was ''turned back'' by stress of weather. (''b''†) To send back; return.
{{smaller block|<poem>We ''turn'' not ''back'' the silks upon the merchant
When we have soil’d them. ''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2. 69.</poem>}}
'''To turn down.''' (''a'') To fold or double down.
{{smaller block|Is not the leaf ''turn’d down?'' {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 3. 273.}}}}
(''b'') To lower by turning a stop-cock or the like: as, to ''turn down'' the gas. (''c'') To snub; suppress. [Slang, U. S.] —'''To turn flukes.''' See ''fluke''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To turn forth,''' to drive or cast out; expel.
{{smaller block|''Turn'' melancholy ''forth'' to funerals. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1. 14.}}}}
'''To turn head†''', to turn round; face about.
{{smaller block|''Turn head'', and stop pursuit. ''Shak.'', Hen. V., ii. 4. 69.}}
'''To turn in.''' (''a'') To fold or double in.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus a wise tailor is not pinching,
But ''turns'' at every seam an inch ''in''.</poem>
{{right|''Hudibras.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}}
(''b'') To turn inward: said especially of the toes.
{{smaller block|I gives ’em the hornpipe and the bandy jig, that’s dancing with my toes ''turned in''. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, III. 200.}}}}
(''c'') To hand over or deliver: as, to ''turn in'' the unexpended balance.—'''To turn in a deadeye''' or '''block,''' to fasten the shroud or strap round the deadeye or block.—'''To turn off.''' (''a'') To dismiss or put away summarily; discard; discharge.
{{smaller block|He ''turned off'' his former wife to make room for this marriage. {{right|''Addison.''}}

Servants sent on messages are apt to stay out somewhat longer than the message requires. . . When you return, the master storms, the lady scolds; stripping, cudgelling, and ''turning off'' is the word. {{right|''Swift'', Advice to Servants (General Directions).}}}} (''b''†) To give over; consign.
{{smaller block|The murmurer is ''turned off'' to the company of those doleful creatures that inhabit the ruins of Babylon.
{{right|''Government of the Tongue.''}}}}
(''c'') To turn aside; divert.
{{smaller block|The institution of sports and shows was intended, by all governments, to ''turn off'' the thoughts of the people from busying themselves in matters of state.
{{right|''Addison'', Freeholder, No. 34.}}}}
(''d'') To perform; accomplish; complete.
{{smaller block|Whatever he may say of its quality, the German official or man of business is always appalled at the quantity of work his compeer here can ''turn off'' in a given time.
{{right|''G. S. Hall'', German Culture, p. 306.}}}}
(''e'') To shut off, as a fluid, by means of a stop-cock, valve, etc., so as to prevent its operation or effect; stop or withdraw the effective supply of: as, to ''turn off'' the gas, the water, or the steam. (''f'') To hang, as a criminal; hence, with humorous allusion to the “noose,” to put through the marriage ceremony; marry. [Slang.]
{{smaller block|Some minutes after he was ''turned off'', a Reprieve came for him, and being immediately cut down, he soon reviv’d, to the admiration of all Spectators.
{{right|''The Flying Post'', Dec. 11, 1705, quoted in Ashton’s Social}}
{{right|[Life in Reign of Queen Anne, II. 215.}}
I saw them ''turned off'' at igsackly a quarter past 12.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Yellowplush Papers, Mr. Deuceace at Paris, ix.}}}}
(''g'') To give a different turn or direction to, or a different meaning or effect to; turn aside: as, to ''turn off'' a joke.—'''To turn on''', to open a passage to, or admit, as a fluid by means of a stop-cock or valve, so as to bring into actual operation or use; bring into play the effective supply of: as, to ''turn on'' the gas, steam, or water.—'''To turn one’s coat''', to change sides; go over to another party, sect, or the like; become a pervert. Compare ''turncoat.''

{{smaller block|They blackguarded him like good ’uns — said he only wanted to get into the House to finger the salary and then ''turn his coat.''
{{right|''Grenville-Murray'', Member for Paris, xx.}}}}
{{smaller block|Mr. Bright should be the last man to charge a political opponent with ''turning his coat.''
{{right|''Westminster Rev.'', CXXVIII. 526.}}}}

'''To turn one’s hand,''' to apply or adapt one’s self.
{{smaller block|A good Servant shou’d ''turn his Hand'' to every thing in a Family.
{{right|''Steele'', Tender Husband, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To all things could he ''turn his hand.''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}

'''To turn one’s head''' or '''brain.''' (''a'') To make one giddy or dizzy, as by looking down from a great height. (''b'') To infect one with extravagant notions, as of pride or conceit: as, the attentions shown him quite ''turned his head.''
{{smaller block|For the benefit of such ''whose heads'' are a little ''turned'', . . . I shall assign one of the sides of the college which I am erecting for the cure of this dangerous distemper [pride].
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 127.}}}}
{{smaller block|The spirit of public fanaticism ''turned their heads.''
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The rush of invitations, and the struggle for his society, . . . would have been quite enough to ''turn any head'' less strong than his.
{{right|''Lady Holland'', Sydney Smith, viii.}}}}

'''To turn out.''' (''a'') To put out; drive out; expel: as, the unruly persons were ''turned out.''
{{smaller block|The triumphant party are not at all in the humour to be ''turned out'' every time his lordship has drunk a bottle too much.
{{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 8.}}}}
(''b'') To put out to pasture, as cattle or horses. (''c'') To produce as the result of labor, or training, or any process of manufacture; furnish in a complete state; send out finished: as, this factory ''turns out'' 1,000 pieces of cloth in a week.
{{smaller block|One thing is very certain — that the [public] schools ''turned out'' splendid scholars, and their powers of writing Latin and Greek verse were wonderful.
{{right|''W. Besant'', Fifty Years Ago, p. 155.}}}} (d) To turn inside out; reverse; hence, to bring to view; show; produce: as, to ''turn out'' one’s pockets; ''turn out'' your cards.—'''To turn over.''' (''a'') To change the position of the top, bottom, or sides of; overturn: as, to ''turn over'' a box; the seats were ''turned over'' in the struggle. (''b'') To hand over; deliver; transfer; refer: as, the business was ''turned over'' to his creditors.
{{smaller block|If he [the footman] be not for your Turn, ''turn'' him ''over'' to me again when I come back.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 13.}}
<poem>’Tis well the debt no payment does demand;
You ''turn'' me ''over'' to another hand.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Aurengzebe, iv. 1.}}}}
(''c'') To do business, or sell goods, to the amount of: as, he ''turns over'' about $1000 a week. (''d'') To open and turn the leaves of for the purpose of examining.
{{smaller block|Some conceive they have no more to do than to ''turn over'' a concordance.
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
(''e''†) To turn off; hang. [Slang.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Criminals, condemned to suffer,
Are blinded first, and then ''turned over.''</poem>
{{right|''S. Butler'', Hudibras, III. ii. 698.}}}}
'''To turn over a new leaf.''' See ''leaf.''—'''To turn tail.''' See ''tail''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To turn the back,''' to turn away; hence, to leave a place or company; go off; run away.
{{smaller block|<poem>Make mouths upon me when I ''turn'' my ''back.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 238.}}
<poem>''Sam.'' Quarrel, I will back thee.
''Gre.'' How! ''turn thy back'' and run?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1. 41.}}}}
'''To turn the back on''' or '''upon one.''' See ''back''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To turn the buckle of the belt behind.''' See ''buckle''<sup>2</sup>.—'''To turn the cat in the pan.''' (''a''†) To reverse the order of things so as to make them appear the opposite of what they really are. ''N. E. D.'', under ''cat.''
{{smaller block|There is a cunning which we in England call “the ''turning of the cat in the pan''”: which is when that which a man says to another he lays it as if another had said it to him.
{{right|''Bacon'', Cunning (ed. 1887).}}}} (''b'') See ''to turn a cat-in-pan'', under ''cat''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To turn the cold shoulder.''' See ''cold''.—'''To turn the die''' or '''the dice,''' to change the luck.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fortune confounds the wise,
And, when they least expect it, ''turns the dice.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''To turn the edge of,''' to deprive of sharpness or keenness; blunt.
{{smaller block|This news, I think, hath ''turn’d'' your weapon’s ''edge.''
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., ii. 1. 179.}}}}
'''To turn the paunch,''' to vomit; disgorge, as fish. [New Eng.]—'''To turn the scale,''' to make one side of the balance fall; hence, figuratively, to give superiority or success; decide; determine.
{{smaller block|You weigh equally; a feather will ''turn the scale.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 2. 32.}}
<poem>If I survive, shall Troy the less prevail?
A single soul ’s too light to ''turn the scale.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''To turn the stomach of,''' to cause nausea or disgust in; make qualmish or disgusted.
{{smaller block|They [Tonquinese] have many sorts of dishes, that wou’d ''turn the Stomach of'' a stranger, which yet they themselves like very well.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, II. i. 30.}}
<poem>This filthy simile, this beastly line,
Quite ''turns my stomach.''</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Epil. to Satires, ii. 182.}}}}
'''To turn the tables.''' See ''table''.—'''To turn tippet†.''' See ''tippet''.—'''To turn to the right-about.''' See ''right-about''.—'''To turn turtle.''' See ''turtle''<sup>2</sup>.—'''To turn up.''' (''a'') To bring to the surface; bring from below to the top; turn over: as, to ''turn up'' the sod or the soil.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yellow “bobs” ''turned up'' before the plough
Are chiefest baits; with cork and lead enough.</poem>
{{right|''J. Dennys'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 176).}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
